I live in the shadow of Lone Peak in the Wasatch Mountains of Utah. I have been with these mountains for more than 50 years. 

When I arrived here we had year-round snow in high crags above 10,000 feet. We had a big glacier on Lone Peak.

It’s gone. 

We had a glacier on Mt. Timpanogos to my south. Gone. There was a substantial glacier on Mt. Nebo that we would climb and ski in the middle of summer. 

Gone. 

The Wasatch run 165 miles north to south from the Idaho border to central Utah. Many of it’s high peaks were snowcapped all year. They are all bare rock now. There have been many slides as the underlying frozen water melted and rocks sheared off. 

We baked away near or above 100 degrees F for three months this summer and had fires all over the place - again. We are running out of water. 

But the Trump crowd says “climate change is a hoax.” 

As he grabs the oil in Venezuela. Oh well. This trend can’t be reversed without a major global die off of humans.

My experience with a family member and also  an ex who were hoarders taught me the power of this disease (and it is a disease). Hoarders don’t want help. 
Sometimes they are ashamed of their situation (as was my ex). Other times they really believe that they need everything they keep (as in my family member).

comments.body: Regarding the threads emerging about global warming and greenhouse gas emissions, we tend to self flagellate in the US. I’m a card carrying Democrat, but the truth is this is a global challenge, and a nuanced one at that. Wealthy countries like Singapore, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Ireland, Norway, and many others (especially Europeans) are responsible for importing more greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions per capita than Americans. America just has a much larger industrial manufacturing sector, and we do consume more total because of our geography and history - newer countries spread across vast land/area including the US, Canada, and Australia have higher combined GHG per capita largely because we drive more (by necessity). Large land mass, newer housing and roads, spread out further than the centuries old cities and villages and cities in Europe. We also build living spaces to heat, cool, and run. So they may suffer through their non AC using summers, but behind the scenes the wealthy Europeans still contribute to the problem. At the end of the day, this is why the “useless” UN exists - global challenges require global coordination. Alas we are too caught up with pointing fingers and also perhaps a hint of lying to ourselves about our ideals vs. needs / reality.

Then about 10 years ago a pamphlet entitled "White Shark Safety on Cape Cod" started being handed out at the admission booths to National Seashore Preserve beaches on the outer Cape (and probably elsewhere).  The first time I saw a pamphlet was at Marconi Beach.  As soon as I got to the beach I saw 5 or 6 seals sunning on a sandbar about 20 feet out from shore.  Without the pamphlet I might not have realized I was looking at a white shark buffet, since the ubiquity of the predators hadn't infiltrated the public mind to the extent that it has since. "Stand up, real big and tall. Shoulders back, chin up. Put a tough swagger in your step and a smirk on your face. Anybody who sees you will think you’re the one who’s going to cause trouble.”

I've followed this wonderful advice all my life. Now, as a petite woman grazing 5' tall, I wouldn't walk anywhere by myself late at night. That said, the ability to project toughness is a useful trait in other settings.

I was trying cases inside courtrooms right after I turned 24 years old. Jurors were often amused at me. I understood that I needed some way to project myself other than "cute little thing". 

This didn't mean projecting anger, hostility. I knew that as a young woman, those qualities would work against me. 

So instead I made it a point to watch the successful litigators. They oozed confidence. They were at ease with themselves. They were comfortable speaking up in public. Then I just started emulating them. 

One more quality - I soon learned that even if I didn't feel that confidence, even if I didn't have all that experience - especially in the first few years - I could fake it really well. And this is when I learned that this is what most of my male colleagues (in those years, they were all men) were doing anyway!

And I knew I succeeded when my daughter, then about 10 years old, told me, "Mom, if you were tall, you'd be really scary!"

Best to everyone here on the MD stoop this morning,

comments.body: In Greensboro, NC we have some ever-present reminders of Maria Edgeworth.  Edgeworth Street is downtown adjacent to the property featuring Blandwood, the mansion of progressive Governor John Motley Morehead (1796-1866).  Morehead had five daughters to educate, and he did so by founding Edgeworth Female Seminary in 1840.  He named the school for the author whose work he greatly admired and to be a significant influence.  Edgeworth and Morehead were convinced that women should have equal intellectual educations, and Morehead brought that conviction into being.  I believe that the school was successful for twenty or more years, but was closed during the Civil War and the building was lost. Edgeworth has indeed been well known and her works have been taught and studied for centuries. She was so popular that her pedagogical works and children's literature sparked a series of schools devoted to her teachings. These schools were not just in Ireland but they were also in the United States--there is a twin in western Pennsylvania that has one, for example. 

She was a great proponent of teaching girls and boys literature, history, languages, and particularly sciences, this in addition to her literary works. I'm thinking of Belinda in which she introduces a character with breast cancer, The Absentee in which she discusses the devastating effects of absentee English colonization on the Irish people and economy, Castle Rackent where she introduces the economic disparities between the generations of landholders and the native Irish as well as the last generation's craven antisemitism. Her Essay on Irish Bulls is an important work on the linguistic and rhetorical differences between English and Irish.

She did not make distinctions between the education of girls and boys. She has been very important in the fields of educational history, Irish history, literature, linguistics, and Jewish studies. Several years ago there was a n exhibit of her books at the Toronto library.

To call her forgotten or erased is simply untrue.

Spanish meals are not the same as those in northern Europe, or the US. The main meal is in the middle of the day at around 2pm. The meal takes a while, it includes socializing and/or family time, and it is followed by some rest (yes, siesta) and a coffee, so you can continue working in the afternoon (at around 4:30 or 5pm). You get a small bite at around 7 (merienda), if hungry, and a small meal at 9:30-10pm when you are back home. At home it could be an omelette and some fruit. If you live in an area with hot weather, you appreciate an hour of siesta when the sun is up! It also slows down your day, which is nice.

When people go out at night with friends or family, then the meals might be larger, and you go to bed later (you need to digest it!), but that is not the daily routine.

1. Major countries with large numbers of ground personnel (like us) don't want to deploy them, for fear of political repercussions when bodies start coming home. So we try to win wars with technology rather than the overwhelming force that is their true advantage. We fight with one hand behind our backs. (China and Russia don't care about this issue, btw.)

2. Countries run by troublesome regimes have gotten better training and weapons for their soldiers and other non-traditional combatants (read: terrorist groups), which has allowed them to get wins here and there, while dragging out the war. That Iran can tie up our multi-million dollar defense systems and muck up Hormuz with $35,000 drones is a great example. 

3. Traditional military advantages are starting to be eroded by cyber expertise. We saw Iran send a cyber message by messing around with some water systems in the midwest. Dolly Parton's passing has all of America ruminating on so many things, but perhaps none more than that she was goodness personified. 

- She earned her impressive living in a fashion that contributed to the arts/entertainment landscape, and harmed no one. 
- She used her well-gotten gains to fund endeavors (literacy, vaccine research, providing band uniforms to underfunded schools) that improved the lives of others, often on a national or global level, but often locally (and anonymously).
- She never turned her back on where she came from.
She did her family, herself, and her church proud.

The demise of small churches that helped produced the likes of her is regrettable in and of itself, but doubly so as these intimate, community gathering places are replaced by megachurches which -- let's be honest -- are essentially tax-free businesses, often wielding outsize political clout.

I hope church-goers (and also regular attendees of synagogues and mosques) can distinguish between the establishments that promote actual goodness (in words and action) and acceptance towards all of humanity, and those that inculcate a sense of superiority and judgment among their members. Only one is worth a contribution into the collection plate.

That Dolly Parton, the extraordinarily gifted and celebrated musician, business woman, actor, songwriter, singer, advocate, is being remembered and loved because of person she was … and the Christian life she lived … well beyond all her “accomplishments,” is an astounding testament to the power of the life she lived, and how she intentionally made every effort to remain kind, strong, grateful, effective and nonjudgmental.

comments.name: Miles Parker
comments.body:
Fascism is at its root an aesthetic movement; yes that aesthetic is derivative, constructed, tedious and violent (see e.g. Futurism), but the point is not only to control people, but to control their perception of reality. It is a game of conspiracies within conspiracies, in which the entire point is to be the one who is most inside the wall. This is why at its heart, all fascist governments have been essentially kleptocracies full of seething, warring interests. It is interesting that we are instead given the image of fascism as .. evil, sure, but also exceptionally efficient and inventive.

Why do I bring this up here? Because fascism obtains its power through the machinery of aesthetic manipulation. It knows that words and actions have real power; yes, to distort reality, to make people believe what you want them to believe.

Now, look at the word magic and the ideology behind Silicon Valley and finance capital in general. It’s a spectacle, full of public and private ritual. The price of entry is to swallow whatever drink you’re given. The reward is to be allowed to put your interests above all others, indeed as the author points out to see those others as hollow shells, meatpuppets that simply provide context and contrast for the only person who actually matters: you.
